==Problem==
Call a positive integer ''fair'' if no digit is used more than once, it has no <imath>0</imath>s, and no digit is adjacent to two greater digits. For example, <imath>196, 23</imath> and <imath>12463</imath> are fair, but <imath>1546, 320,</imath> and <imath>34321</imath> are not. How many fair positive integers are there?
 
<imath>\textbf{(A) } 511 \qquad \textbf{(B) } 2584 \qquad \textbf{(C) } 9841 \qquad \textbf{(D) } 17711 \qquad \textbf{(E) } 19682</imath>

==Solution 1==

To satisfy the conditions, a fair integer must have no digit be a local minimum. Let's say we have <imath>n</imath> distinct digits, with each digit being a number from <imath>1</imath> to <imath>9</imath>. To create a fair integer, we begin by placing the largest digit. For the second-largest digit, we can either place this digit to the right or to the left of the string already created. We have these <imath>2</imath> options for the third-largest digit, and so on. Therefore, there are <imath>2^{n-1}</imath> valid permutations to create a fair integer.
 
We must also choose which digits will be in the permutation. If you are creating an <imath>n</imath>-digit long fair integer, there are <imath>\binom{9}{n}</imath> ways to pick which digits will be in the number.
 
Therefore, for each <imath>n \in \{1,2,\dots, 9\}</imath>, the number of fair integers of length <imath>n</imath> is:
<cmath>\binom{9}{n} \cdot 2^{n-1}.</cmath>
Summing over all <imath>n</imath>:
<cmath>\sum_{n=1}^9{\binom{9}{n} \cdot 2^{n-1}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\sum_{n=0}^9{\binom{9}{n}}2^n -1\right)=\frac{1}{2}\left((1+2)^9 -1 \right) = \frac{1}{2}(19682) = \boxed{9841}.</cmath>
Note that the Binomial Theorem was used to equate
<cmath>\sum_{n=0}^9{\binom{9}{n}}2^n = (1+2)^9.</cmath>
~lprado

==Solution 2==

Note every fair number will have an increasing string of digits, a maximum digit, then a decreasing string of digits. This is because if it decreases then increases, then the digit in the middle will be less than its adjacent digits.

Let <imath>n</imath> be the maximum digit. For each number <imath>i<n</imath>, we may either place <imath>i</imath> before <imath>n</imath>, after <imath>n</imath>, or choose not to include it. Note this process will result in a unique number for every case, as the numbers before <imath>n</imath> must be in increasing order, and the numbers after <imath>n</imath> must be in decreasing order. Therefore, for each number <imath>n</imath>, we have <imath>3^{n-1}</imath> cases.

Since <imath>n \in \{1,2,\cdots9\}</imath>, we have:
<cmath>\sum_{n=1}^9 3^{n-1}=\frac{3^9-1}{3-1}=\boxed{9841}.</cmath>
 
~SilverRush

== Solution 3 (Recursion)==
Let <imath>f(n)</imath> be the number of fair integers given an arbitrary set of <imath>n</imath> digits. Let <imath>a</imath> be the smallest of these digits. Notice that <imath>a</imath> is either the first or last digit, as if it were any other digit, the two digits surrounding it would both be greater. Then, notice that if the remaining <imath>n-1</imath> slots form a fair number, so does the number when <imath>a</imath> is appended. Therefore, <imath>f(n) = 2f(n-1)</imath>. From here, we may proceed with the calculation in Solution <imath>1</imath> to get the answer of <imath>\boxed {\text {(C) } 9841}</imath>

~ Shadowleafy

== Solution 4 ==

For any fair integer <imath>n</imath>, we write some <imath>9</imath>-digit base-<imath>3</imath> number(s) <imath>f(n)=\left(\overline{d_1 d_2 \ldots d_9}\right)_3</imath> from left to right as follows:

* <imath>d_k=0</imath> if <imath>k</imath> is not in <imath>n</imath>;
* <imath>d_k=1</imath> if <imath>k</imath> is the to the left of all digits greater than <imath>k</imath> in <imath>n</imath>;
* <imath>d_k=2</imath> if <imath>k</imath> is the to the right of all digits greater than <imath>k</imath> in <imath>n</imath>.

Note that the fairness ensured one and only one of the above three cases happens. 

Now if <imath>k</imath> is the largest digit in <imath>n</imath> then <imath>d_k</imath> can be either <imath>1</imath> or <imath>2</imath>.

An example: If <imath>n=136852</imath>, then <imath>f(n)=\overline{121021010}_3</imath> or <imath>\overline{121021020}_3</imath>. 

It's thus easy to see that there is a <imath>1</imath>-to-<imath>2</imath> mapping from all fair integers to all <imath>9</imath>-digit base-<imath>3</imath> nonzero numbers. Therefore the answer is <imath>\frac{3^9-1}{2}</imath>.


~ asops
